THE CORE IDEA

runs.text: Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.

WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPARING TAX BURDENS

runs.text: The horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. A downward-sloping demand curve intersects the original upward-sloping supply curve at price $15 and quantity 100. A parallel curve labeled Supply plus tax lies above supply and intersects demand at price $18 and quantity 80. At quantity 80 the original supply curve is at $12; dashed guides also mark quantities 65, 120, and 150 and prices $10 and $20.

transcript.text: The horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. A downward-sloping demand curve intersects the original upward-sloping supply curve at price $15 and quantity 100. A parallel curve labeled Supply plus tax lies above supply and intersects demand at price $18 and quantity 80. At quantity 80 the original supply curve is at $12; dashed guides also mark quantities 65, 120, and 150 and prices $10 and $20.

transcript.sourceText: The untaxed equilibrium price is $15. With the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. Buyers bear $18 - $15 = $3 per unit, so their total burden is $3 x 80 = $240. Sellers bear the remaining $3 per unit.
transcript.text: The untaxed equilibrium price is 15 dollars . With the tax, buyers pay 18 dollars , sellers receive 12 dollars , and 80 units are sold. Buyers bear 18 dollars minus 15 dollars equals 3 dollars per unit, so their total burden is 3 dollars times 80 equals 240 dollars . Sellers bear the remaining 3 dollars per unit.
